paras: The burning of an Indian woman near Port Ludlow was a reported burning at the stake in Washington Territory in late November 1888, in which a young Native woman said members of her own tribe had tied her to a stake and set her afire. She survived with severe burns and was taken to the county poor house at Port Townsend. The story ran on the wire as far as New York and Delaware, but a later local report attributed her burns to relatives attempting a customary cure.

On the morning of November 25, a man named Price brought the woman to the Port Townsend poor house, burned from her lower body to just below the neck. He said he had found her nude on the beach near Port Ludlow, and that she told him in broken Chinook that "male and female members of her tribe" had stripped her the evening before, tied her to a stake, piled brushwood around it, lit it and left her to die. According to the wire version, she freed herself by "herculean efforts"; that version gave her age as 19.

The cause was not established. Price judged from her "random remarks" that she was being punished for having contracted a "loathsome disease", a claim later wire copies presented as the "alleged reason."

On December 4 the Post-Intelligencer's Port Townsend correspondent gave a different account, placing her discovery near Port Discovery. It had "since been learned," the letter said, that her relatives had tried to cure her probable rheumatism "after their usual custom" with fire or heated irons, and that the ordeal had destroyed her reason. Probate Judge Whittlesey was to examine her for commitment to the asylum once her burns healed, and no report of arrests appears in the coverage.

The Seattle Post-Intelligencer broke the story under the headline "A Young Squaw Burned at the Stake," while cautioning that its truth could not be ascertained that night, though the informant spoke with "apparent truthfulness." Wire versions reached the Los Angeles Herald, under "Redskin Barbarity," and the Sacramento Record-Union, under "An Indian Outrage," within two days, and dropped the reporter's doubts. The Arizona Weekly Citizen ran the same dispatch on December 1, and reprints under "Burned at the Stake" appeared in Butte on December 19 and in Milford, Delaware, on December 28.

A Tacoma paper, reprinted in the New York Evening World, called the account a tale of medieval barbarity that could hardly be believed until verified, given how close it was to "enlightened communities." None of the distant reprints carried the December 4 correction.

The two explanations rest on different sources: the first on a finder's reading of the woman's words in broken Chinook, the second on what the Port Townsend correspondent said had been learned afterward. The reports also differ on where she was found, Port Ludlow or Port Discovery, and the Post-Intelligencer's printed age reads "about 12" against 19 in the wire copies.

reader.title: Burning of an Indian woman near Port Ludlow
bases: The first wire account described an Indian woman tied to a stake and burned by members of her own tribe who left her to perish, an attempted killing by a group (A2, A4), but the later local Port Townsend letter attributed the burns to relatives trying to cure her illness by fire or heated irons (A6); she survived, and no white or Black party was involved.

The woman survived her burns and was taken to the county poor house (A2, A6), so no one was killed; whether the burning was a punishment for disease (A2, A9) or a customary cure (A6) is disputed, and the number of people involved is not given.

All November reports trace to one Post-Intelligencer special relaying the finder's account of the woman's words (A2, A3, A4, A9), and the same paper's Dec. 4 Port Townsend letter gave a different explanation, a cure attempt by relatives (A6).
